```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: true
source(here::here("R", "setup.R"))
walk  <- load_walk()
clear <- load_clear()
diary <- load_diary()
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Simulated data"}
All examples use simulated data from fictional studies. Results illustrate methods; they are not empirical findings.
:::

These exercises practise the diagnostic and troubleshooting skills of Module 11: reading conditional and marginal residuals, measuring the influence of participants, judging random-effects assumptions, simulation-based residuals for GLMMs, responding to warnings and separation, and recording decisions in an analysis log. Code chunks contain blanks (`___`) and are set to `eval: false` so that the workbook renders before you complete them. Fill in the blanks and run the chunks interactively, or change them to `eval: true`.

Exercise G2 uses the leave-one-participant-out results saved by `scripts/11_diagnostics.R` in `outputs/models/m11_loo.rds`. If the file is missing, run that script first (it takes several minutes). The analysis log template is in `admin/templates/analysis_log_template.md`.

## Guided exercises

### Exercise G1. Conditional and marginal residuals for the linear-time model (LO 11.1)

The linear-time WALK model is `lmer(sbp ~ month * arm + (1 + month | id))`. It assumes that mean SBP changes linearly over the 12 months in each arm.

(a) Fit the model and add conditional fitted values, marginal fitted values, standardised conditional residuals and marginal residuals to the data.

```{r}
#| eval: false
m_lin <- lmer(sbp ~ month * arm + (1 + month | id), data = walk,
              control = lmer_ctrl)
res_lin <- walk |>
  mutate(fit_cond = fitted(___),
         fit_marg = predict(m_lin, re.form = ___),
         res_cond_std = resid(m_lin, scaled = ___),
         res_marg = sbp - ___)
```

(b) Plot the marginal residuals against actual time, coloured by arm, with a loess smoother for each arm.

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(res_lin, aes(month, ___, colour = arm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Actual time (months)", y = "Marginal residual (mmHg)")
```

(c) Make the same plot for the standardised conditional residuals.

(d) Questions. (i) Describe the pattern of the marginal residuals over time in the programme arms. What does it tell you about the linear-time mean model? (ii) Does the pattern also appear in the conditional residuals? Can random slopes absorb a curvature that is shared by everyone in an arm? (iii) Would you use the linear-time model to estimate the month-3 difference between EP and UC?

### Exercise G2. Influential participants (LO 11.1)

(a) Read the cached leave-one-out results and compute the change in the EP − UC difference at month 12 as a fraction of its standard error.

```{r}
#| eval: false
m_pri <- lmer(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id), data = walk,
              control = lmer_ctrl)
loo <- readRDS(here("outputs", "models", "m11_loo.rds"))
se_ep12 <- sqrt(vcov(m_pri)["visit_f12:armEP", "visit_f12:armEP"])
loo <- loo |>
  mutate(dfbeta = fixef(m_pri)["visit_f12:armEP"] - ___,
         frac_se = abs(dfbeta) / ___) |>
  left_join(walk |> distinct(id, arm), by = "id") |>
  arrange(desc(frac_se))
head(loo, 5)
```

(b) Plot the observed SBP trajectories of the three most influential participants over the arm mean trajectories.

```{r}
#| eval: false
top3 <- loo$id[1:3]
arm_means <- walk |> group_by(arm, month_sched) |> summarise(sbp = mean(sbp))
ggplot(filter(walk, id %in% ___), aes(month, sbp, group = id)) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = arm), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = arm_means, aes(month_sched, sbp, group = arm, colour = arm),
            linetype = 2) +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Months", y = "SBP (mmHg)")
```

(c) Refit the primary model without the most influential participant and confirm the change in the estimate.

```{r}
#| eval: false
m_drop <- lmer(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id),
               data = filter(walk, id != ___), control = lmer_ctrl)
fixef(m_drop)["visit_f12:armEP"]
```

(d) Questions. (i) What makes the most influential participants influential? (ii) Would any of them justify a sensitivity analysis under the rule "a participant who changes a primary contrast by more than half its standard error"? (iii) Why is influence measured by participant rather than by observation?

### Exercise G3. BLUPs and shrinkage (LO 11.2)

(a) Compute, for a random-intercept model fitted to WALK, the shrinkage factor $\lambda_i = \tau_0^2/(\tau_0^2 + \sigma^2/n_i)$ for $n_i = 1, \dots, 6$.

```{r}
#| eval: false
m_ri <- lmer(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 | id), data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)
tau0_sq  <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_ri))$vcov[1]
sigma_sq <- sigma(m_ri)^___
data.frame(n_i = 1:6, lambda = tau0_sq / (tau0_sq + sigma_sq / ___))
```

(b) Compare the SD of the predicted random intercepts with the estimated $\tau_0$, separately for participants with fewer than 4 and with 6 observations.

```{r}
#| eval: false
blup <- data.frame(id = rownames(ranef(m_ri)$id), b0 = ranef(m_ri)$id[, 1]) |>
  left_join(count(walk, id, name = "n_i"), by = "id")
blup |> mutate(group = ifelse(n_i < 4, "fewer than 4", ifelse(n_i == 6, "6", "4-5"))) |>
  group_by(group) |> summarise(n = n(), sd_blup = sd(___))
sqrt(tau0_sq)
```

(c) Questions. (i) Why is the SD of the BLUPs smaller than $\hat\tau_0$, and why does the gap depend on $n_i$? (ii) A colleague says "the Q–Q plot of the BLUPs is straight, so the random intercepts are normal". What would you reply?

### Exercise G4. Simulation-based residuals for DIARY (LO 11.3)

(a) Fit Poisson and negative binomial GLMMs for migraine days, with log(`days`) as an offset, and compute DHARMa residuals with 500 simulations.

```{r}
#| eval: false
m_pois <- glmmTMB(migraine_days ~ arm * post + offset(log(___)) + (1 | id),
                  family = poisson, data = diary)
m_nb   <- glmmTMB(migraine_days ~ arm * post + offset(log(days)) + (1 | id),
                  family = ___, data = diary)
s_pois <- simulateResiduals(m_pois, n = 500, seed = 1)
s_nb   <- simulateResiduals(m_nb, n = 500, seed = 1)
plot(s_pois)
testDispersion(s_pois, plot = FALSE); testZeroInflation(s_pois, plot = FALSE)
testDispersion(s_nb, plot = FALSE);   testZeroInflation(s_nb, plot = FALSE)
```

(b) Aggregate the negative binomial residuals by participant and test dispersion with conditional and with unconditional simulation.

```{r}
#| eval: false
s_nb_u <- simulateResiduals(m_nb, n = 500, seed = 1, simulateREs = ___)
testDispersion(recalculateResiduals(s_nb, group = diary$id), plot = FALSE)
testDispersion(recalculateResiduals(s_nb_u, group = ___), plot = FALSE)
```

(c) Questions. (i) Which model would you use and why? (ii) Is a zero-inflated model needed? (iii) Which participant-level result should you trust, and why?

### Exercise G5. Rescaling, `allFit()` and sparse data (LO 11.4)

(a) Fit the linear-time WALK model with time in **weeks** (`month * 4.348`) and age in years, and with time in months and age per 10 years. Compare the EP slope difference per month and any warnings.

```{r}
#| eval: false
walk_w <- walk |> mutate(week = month * 4.348, age10 = (age - 60) / 10)
m_w <- lmer(sbp ~ week * arm + age + (1 + week | id), data = walk_w,
            control = lmer_ctrl)
m_m <- lmer(sbp ~ month * arm + age10 + (1 + month | id), data = walk_w,
            control = lmer_ctrl)
c(weeks = fixef(m_w)["week:armEP"] * ___, months = fixef(m_m)["month:armEP"])
```

(b) Run `allFit()` on the months model. Write the control argument out in full (or leave it out): `allFit()` cannot evaluate the shared `lmer_ctrl` object stored in the model call.

```{r}
#| eval: false
m_m2 <- lmer(sbp ~ month * arm + age10 + (1 + month | id), data = walk_w,
             control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
af <- summary(allFit(m_m2, verbose = FALSE))
af$llik; af$fixef[, "month:armEP"]
```

(c) In CLEAR, tabulate moderate-or-severe itch by arm at week 12 among participants with **severe** itch (severity 3) at baseline. Is any cell sparse?

```{r}
#| eval: false
sev3 <- clear |> filter(week == 0, severity == ___) |> pull(id)
clear |> filter(id %in% sev3, week == 12) |> count(arm, itch)
```

(d) Questions. (i) Was the warning in (a), if any, a sign of a real problem? How do you know? (ii) What would you do if a subgroup analysis of the CLEAR treatment effect had a cell with no events?

### Exercise G6. Analysis log entries (LO 11.6)

Using `admin/templates/analysis_log_template.md`, write two complete log entries for decisions made in Exercises G4 and G5: (1) the choice between the Poisson and negative binomial model; (2) the rescaling of time and age. Fill every field, including **Status** and **Effect on estimates**.

## Independent exercises

### Exercise I1. GEE mean-model check for DIARY (LO 11.3)

Fit a GEE for the DIARY migraine-day counts with a log link, Poisson variance function, `offset(log(days))`, an exchangeable working correlation and `arm * period_f` as the mean model. Compare it with a model using `arm * post`. Plot observed and fitted mean rates (migraine days per diary day) by period and arm, and plot Pearson residuals by period. Is `arm * post` an adequate mean model? Use QIC as one piece of evidence.

### Exercise I2. Separation and penalised likelihood (LO 11.4)

Simulate a trial with 30 participants per arm, three post-baseline visits and a rare binary event (baseline log-odds −2.5), in which the active arm has no events after baseline. Fit the logistic model `event ~ active * post` by maximum likelihood, by Firth's method (use the `firth_logit()` function from the notes) and with `glmmTMB` with a `normal(0, 2.5)` prior and a random intercept. Report the three estimates of the interaction and explain which you would report and how.

### Exercise I3. Responding to diagnostics (LO 11.5)

For each scenario, write a short paragraph saying what you would do, what you would not do, and what you would record in the analysis log.

(a) In a two-arm trial, the residual variance of the outcome at the final visit is twice that at baseline. The pre-specified model assumes constant variance.

(b) After fitting the pre-specified model, a colleague suggests removing the random slope "because the p-value for the treatment effect becomes significant without it".

(c) One participant's month-12 SBP is 92 mmHg, 60 mmHg lower than at their previous visit, and removing them changes the EP − UC contrast by 0.8 of its SE.

### Exercise I4. Non-normal random effects with sparse data (LO 11.2)

Using `sim_re_shape()` from the notes, repeat the random-effects simulation with 30 participants per arm and only three visits (0, 6 and 12 months), with 100 simulated trials per distribution. Report bias, empirical SE, mean model-based SE and coverage with Monte Carlo SEs. Does the conclusion of the notes still hold? What limits what you can conclude?
